records.name: Betti
records.facts_used: The Estonian dictionary explicitly explains Betti as a diminutive of Eliisabet. The base-name family connects with Hebrew ēlīšeba, my God is an oath, and Greek Elisabet. Independent use of a short form preserves this relationship with the full name. The University of Tartu writers’ dictionary names the poet Betti (Elisabet) Alver. It dates Tuulearmuke to 1927 and her first poetry collection Tolm ja tuli to 1936. A particular author’s biography thus illustrates the connection between short and full forms.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicit family evidence and a concrete historical, bibliographic, calendar, literary or professional episode support two paragraphs in all five languages.
records.uncertainties: Exact Estonian Wiktionary derives from Eliisabet. Opened Tartu EWOD explicitly names Betti (Elisabet) Alver, dates Tuulearmuke to 1927 and first poetry collection Tolm ja tuli to 1936. It is a documented individual full/short pair, not universal evidence for other countries’ Betti uses.

records.name: Eliise
records.facts_used: The Estonian dictionary entry explains Eliise as a short form of Eliisabet. The base-name family connects with Hebrew ēlīšeba, my God is an oath, and Greek Elisabet. Independent use of a short form preserves this relationship with the full name. Péter Pomozi and Eszter Földesi’s 2016 study illustrates this Estonian family’s formation patterns: its table places short and affectionate forms beneath full Elisabeth, Elisabet and Elizabet. It is a concrete linguistic account of the family rather than the first registration date of each modern spelling.

records.uncertainties: Exact Estonian Wiktionary entry explicitly shortens Eliisabet. The 2016 EE-POMOZI16 paper, PDF p. 10 / printed p. 202, Table 1, was visually checked. It documents the related family’s full Elisabeth/Elisabet/Elizabet and derivative structures, but its Elise is not silently renamed Eliise. Story is scoped to family history, not an exact Eliise first record.

records.name: Audronė
records.facts_used: Audronė is a Lithuanian name that the guide derives from Audra and the common noun audra, storm or strong wind. This natural phenomenon explains the name’s formation. It does not imply that every bearer must have a stormy or restless personality. Salys’s essay on Lithuanian names includes Audronė among examples of new formations; the checked text was reprinted in 1983. A named bearer is violinist Audronė Vainiūnaitė, who played first violin in the Vilnius Quartet from 1965 to 2015. These illustrate different linguistic and cultural parts of the name’s history.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicit family evidence and a concrete historical, bibliographic, calendar, literary or professional episode support two paragraphs in all five languages.
records.uncertainties: Exact LT-GUIDE gives Audra/audra storm. Visually checked Salys PDF p. 284 / printed p. 269 includes Audronė among creative noun/adjective-based calendar names. Checked publication is the 1983 reprint, not a coining year. Opened VLE Audronė Vainiūnaitė records first violin in Vilnius Quartet 1965–2015.

His profession is a biographical fact rather than a quality inferred from the name.

records.name: Matilda
records.facts_used: Matilda belongs to the Germanic Mahthilt family, with maht, strength or might, and hilt, battle. This two-part structure belongs to the earlier form and survives in the explanation of its origin. Spellings in different European languages reflect the family’s subsequent spread. The 1964 name calendar reprinted by Salys lists Matilda with short forms Mata and Tilda on 19 November. This is a concrete record of the full name and two short forms in the 1983 volume. It does not claim that both short forms must arise only from Matilda in every family.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicit family evidence and a concrete historical, bibliographic, calendar, literary or professional episode support two paragraphs in all five languages.
records.uncertainties: LT-GUIDE’s prose gives Germanic Mathilda, meht/hild, corroborated by curated Matilda maht/hilt; guide’s separate Hebrew-origin metadata contradicts its prose and was rejected.
